profile.summary: 2 Kings presents the history of the kings of the divided kingdom of Israel and Judah, evaluating each government by faithfulness to the Lord. The book highlights the spiritual failure of many kings, who led their nations to judgment, but also shows some remarkable examples of trust in God, respect for his word and zeal for the covenant. The narrative goes from the last days of the northern kingdom, through the fall of Samaria, to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile, ending with brief notes on Judah after the fall of the city and the late deliverance of Joaquim. The work was probably completed shortly after 586 BC, although the exact authorship is unknown; there is tradition that associates it with Jeremiah, but this remains uncertain.
profile.setting: The book continues the story begun in 1 Kings, in the context of the divided monarchy: Israel to the north and Judah to the south. Part of the narrative occurs in the final periods of the two kingdoms, until the fall of Israel in 722 BC and Judah in 586 BC. The scene is strongly marked by the succession of kings, by the performance of the prophets Elijah and Elisha, by the threat of regional powers such as Assyria and Babylon, and by the centrality of the people's relationship with the covenant of the Lord.

structure.label: Transition from Elijah to Elisha
structure.description: Death of Ahaziah of Israel, the end of Elijah's earthly ministry and the beginning of Elisha's performance, with his first acts and miracles.

structure.label: Conflicts of thrones and initial reforms
structure.description: Reigned in Judah and Israel until the turn of 841 BC, including the ascension of Jehu, the elimination of the house of Ahab, and the taking of the throne of Judah by Athaliah, followed by the restoration of Joash.

structure.label: Decline and fall of the northern kingdom
structure.description: Stage of instability in Israel, with brief and successive reigns, culminating in the unfaithful politics of Hosea, the fall of Samaria and in the analysis of the motives of the ruin of the northern kingdom.

structure.label: The reign of Hezekiah in Judah
structure.description: Hezekiah stands out for relying on the Lord under pressure, although the text also records its flaws at later times.

structure.label: Final break and reform of Josias
structure.description: Manasseh and other kings promote wickedness and idolatry, until Josiah stands out for devotion to the law of the Lord and for the reformation of worship.

structure.label: Fall of Jerusalem and final notes
structure.description: The last kings of Judah do evil, Jerusalem is destroyed by Babylon, and the book concludes with appendices about the events after the fall and deliverance of Jehoiachin.

themes: Fidelity or infidelity to the word of God
Hope and approval linked to trust in the Lord
readingKeys: Notice how each king is evaluated: the pattern is not political success, but what was right or bad in the eyes of the Lord.
Note the role of Elijah and Elisha as spokesmen of God in the midst of national failure.
Read the fall of Israel and Judah as a result of unfaithfulness to the covenant, and compare the kings who received praise with those who were condemned.
profile.cautions: The exact authorship is unknown; the tradition that attributes the book to Jeremiah is not consensual. Absolute dates depend on the comparison with records of neighboring peoples, and the source presented offers a probable historical reconstruction, not an undeniable chronology. The book should not only be read as a list of kings, but as a theological narrative that interprets history in the light of the covenant with God.

dossier.narratedEra: The narrated time ranges from the beginning of the reign of Ahaziah of Israel and the divided monarchy (with Jehoshaphat in Judah) until the fall of Samaria, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the later deliverance of Jehoiachin into Babylon. The explicit historical frame in the notes covers the crisis of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the ascension of Jehu, the pressure of Aramy, the Assyrian expansion, the Babylonian advance and exile.
dossier.compositionEra: The final essay is presented in the notes as the work of a single author of 1-2 Kings, of unknown identity, well-informed about sources and about the late history of Judah. The confessional source proposes that the final composition of 2 Kings occurred shortly after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, with the final appendix added shortly after the death of Nebuchadnezzar II (after 562 BC). The tradition mentioned identifies this author with Jeremiah, but this is presented as a tradition, not as certainty; there is also the possibility of a later addition in 25:27-30.

politics.title: Monarchy divided as a permanent political framework
politics.detail: The book continues the story of the divided monarchy, beginning with Ahaziah reigning in the north and Josaphat in the south. The notes read 2 Kings as a record of the "fortunas" of two kingdoms that go towards distinct outcomes.
politics.readingImpact: This prevents an isolated reading from each kingdom: the narrative constantly compares Israel and Judah and evaluates its stability for fidelity to the covenant.

politics.title: Moabite independence after the death of Ahab
politics.detail: At the outset, the Moabites consider the opportune time to declare independence from Israeli rule after Ahab's death.
politics.readingImpact: The episode shows that a king's death could quickly destabilize Israel's regional hegemony.

politics.title: Jeú, the crisis of 841 BC and the collapse of Ahab's house
politics.detail: The notes are 841 BC as a decisive year: Jehu kills Jorão and Acazias, executes Jezebel, the survivors of Ahab's family and the officers linked to the worship of Baal. Then his long reign began in Israel; at the same time, Athaliah usurps the throne of Judah until the enthronement of Joash.
politics.readingImpact: The reading begins to see political violence as a providential turn and also as a judgment against an idolatrous dynasty.

politics.title: Pressure aramea and the paper of Hazael
politics.detail: The royal Aramean house in Damascus continues to oppress Israel. Hazael takes the throne through the murder of Ben-hadad II and maintains pressure on the north; later Ben-hadad son of Hazael reigns over a declining kingdom.
politics.readingImpact: Israel appears politically weakened and militarily vulnerable, so that liberation comes only when God intervenes, not by internal force.

politics.title: Assyria, Egypt and the fall of the north
politics.detail: Hosea, last king of Israel, trusts in Egypt, and rebels against Assyria; this leads to the capture of Samaria and the end of the northern kingdom in 722 BC. The notes also point to the Adade-Nirari III campaign as a relevant element in the weakening arameu.
politics.readingImpact: Foreign policy is read theologically: poorly valued human alliances and calculated rebellions do not replace trust in YHWH.

politics.title: Babylon, Siege of Jerusalem and residual administration in Judah
politics.detail: Nebuchadonosor II destroys Jerusalem; Ribla functions as Babylonian headquarters; then Gedaliah governs the remaining population in Mispah until his assassination. The closure also mentions the benign treatment given to Joaquim by Evil-Merodaque.
politics.readingImpact: Judah is not only militarily defeated; it also enters a period of administrative reorganization and population displacement that explains the final tone of exile and hope.

customs.title: Household apparatus: upper room with lattice
customs.detail: The note on 2 Kings 1:2 describes a upper room or trellis with trellis as a common structure, useful for ventilation and privacy, but vulnerable to breakage.
customs.readingImpact: The domestic detail makes the accident of Ahaziah more concrete and shows the fragility of the royal dwelling.

customs.title: Military units of fifty
customs.detail: The "fifty people" appear as a common military grouping in the notes on Elijah's confrontation with the captains sent by Ahaziah.
customs.readingImpact: The episode gains a state military organization fund, not just personal confrontation between the prophet and king.

customs.title: Temple as a renovation and maintenance center
customs.detail: The notes highlight that certain kings of Judah care about the repair and maintenance of the Temple, including Joash and Josiah.
customs.readingImpact: The royal piety is also assessed by concrete investment in central cult, not only by religious statements.

customs.title: Agricultural work of the remaining poor
customs.detail: After the Babylonian conquest, the poorest are left in Judah because they would hardly offer resistance; they stay to work in the vineyards and fields.
customs.readingImpact: The fall of Jerusalem has a visible social effect: depopulation of the elites and the permanence of an economically vulnerable population to local livelihood.

customs.title: Ride Worship: Baal and Ideal
customs.detail: The notes describe the cult of Baal as the religious error inherited from Ahab and mention Aserah's post-idol as a Canaanite symbol of fertility that remained after the purge of Jehu.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to read the book as a dispute between fidelity to YHWH and competing cult practices within Israel itself.

customs.title: Dispoof of temple objects and elite exile
customs.detail: The Babylonians dismantle Temple utensils for their own use and deport the majority of the population; important leaders are executed instead of only deported.
customs.readingImpact: The desecration of the sanctuary and the removal of sacred goods reinforce the sense of national humiliation and cultual rupture.

language.title: "Baal-zebube" as possible pejorative pun
language.detail: The note proposes that Baal-zebub (the light of the flies) may be a parody of Baal-zebul, and notes that the name was later used for Satan in another biblical context.
language.readingImpact: The name of the god of Etron is not neutral; the narrative already embute irony and criticism of foreign worship.

language.title: Man of God as marker of prophetic authority
language.detail: The notes explain that the expression "man of God" indicates a prophet whose authority comes from God, so that disobeying him amounts to despising God himself.
language.readingImpact: Prophetic speech ceases to be a generic religious council and becomes a word with divine authority.

language.title: The Fire as the image of the divine presence
language.detail: The fire is presented as a recurring symbol of God's presence in the Scriptures, appearing in the episode of Elijah.
language.readingImpact: The miracle is not just a spectacle; it communicates presence, judgment and authentication of the prophetic word.

language.title: Formula of the kings
language.detail: The introduction highlights the recurrence of the assessments "feves what was bad" and "feves what was right in the eyes of the Lord."
language.readingImpact: The narrative focus is not only on political achievements, but in moral and pactual judgment.

language.title: Cars and knights of Israel" as the language of prophetic succession
language.detail: The expression used by Elisha when saying goodbye to Elijah is treated as a figurative tribute to the spiritual importance of the prophet.
language.readingImpact: Language shifts the confidence of military power to the true spiritual force represented by Elijah/Elysseus.

language.title: Literary structure with final annexes episodes
language.detail: The notes note that the last verses function as two short appendices: reorganization in Judah and the elevation of Jehoiachin in Babylon.
language.readingImpact: The closure becomes more open than a final of mere defeat; he suggests continuity of the story after exile.

timeline.title: Starting point of the narrative: the beginning of the post-Auquilate crisis
timeline.detail: The note of 1:17 links the reign of Ahaziah to 852 BC, in the second year of Jehoram, within a correction with Jehoshaphat dated 853-848 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology shows that the book works with realm overlays; this affects the reading of dates and avoids linear simplifications.

timeline.title: Mark of 841 BC and ascension of Jehu
timeline.detail: The notes mark 841 BC as the year in which Jehu eliminates Joram and Ahaziah, begins his reign and the usurpation of Atalia in Judah begins until the installation of Joash.
timeline.readingImpact: This year functions as a political and theological turn for the two kingdoms.

timeline.title: Jeoacaz and the pressure aramean in 814-798 BC.
timeline.detail: Jehoahaz is dated from 814 to 798 BC; his reign occurs amid the oppression of Aramy and the military weakness of Israel.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronological interval helps to read 2 Kings 13 as a section of national decline and dependence on divine mercy.

timeline.title: Assyrian cycle and indentation arameus in 805-802 BC.
timeline.detail: The notes connect the western advance of Adade-Nirari III (805-802 BC) the capture of Damascus in 802 BC, a scenario that allows Israel some relief under Jehoash.
timeline.readingImpact: Israel's partial victory is explained amid changes in regional power, not as full autonomy.

timeline.title: Fall of Samaria in 722 BC
timeline.detail: The north ends in 722 BC, when Hosea rebels against Assyria, Samaria is taken, and the kingdom of Israel comes to an end.
timeline.readingImpact: The destruction of the northern kingdom is read as a culmination of decades of infidelity, not as an isolated accident.

timeline.title: Fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC and later appendix
timeline.detail: The notes place the final composition just after 586 BC, with the final appendix probably added after the death of Nebuchadnezzar II in 562 BC; the liberation of Joaquim is dated from 561 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The end of the book preserves memory of the disaster, but also a small opening of hope in exile.

timeline.title: Later return in 538 BC as a horizon of hope
timeline.detail: The note of 25:21 mentions that a remnant returned to the land in 538 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: Although this is beyond the main storyline of 2 Kings, the given functions as a performative horizon of restoration.

investigation: The attached sources mainly cover the general introduction and selective notes of 1, 13 and 25; therefore, the historical-cultural reconstruction is concentrated in narrative frameworks and the seized excerpts.
The traditional authorship of Jeremiah is mentioned, but the main source keeps the author as unknown; I treated tradition as tradition and critical authorship as indeterminate.
Absolute dates appear as timeline correlations provided by the notes; I did not use external chronologies or their own harmonizations beyond what the secondary source explicitly states.

Some important themes of 2 Kings - internal administration, popular life in many regions, daily economy and liturgical practices outside the commented stretches - are not sufficiently detailed in the attached notes.

The explicit-source/interpretation/debated ratings reflect the very way the notes speak: when the note directly states, I marked explicit-source; when there is editorial inference, usei interpretation; and controversies were only marked when the source itself indicated them.
dossier.limits: This dossier is necessarily selective because it depends only on the attached notes provided, not the full text of 2 Kings or other reference works. Sections about customs and language have closer coverage than politics and chronology, as the available notes focus on specific episodes (1, 13 and 25) and a short introduction. Authorship, date and certain chronologies remain at the level of proposal or tradition, not of absolute certainty. I also did not add independent historical reconstructions on events not explicitly mentioned in the notes, to avoid mixing the biblical plot with information not supported by the attached sources.
